title: Over-relax the viewport sphere tracer so scaled fields stop dropping out
abstract:
Mitigates #76 (does not close it — see below).

## Problem

A non-uniform `scale` multiplies the child distance field by `min(sx,sy,sz)` — the correct 1-Lipschitz correction — so a scaled subtree under-reports distance by up to `max(scale)/min(scale)`. The fixed-budget marcher in `SdfMesh.ts` (256 steps, stepping `t += abs(d) * 0.7`) then needs that many times the usual step count, and rays that exhaust the budget fall through to `discard`: valid geometry silently vanishes at grazing angles and reappears as you orbit back.

## Change

Enhanced sphere tracing (Keinert et al. 2014): over-relax the step by `omega = 1.6`, and retreat when the over-relaxed step overshoots the field's safe radius. The backtrack lands back inside the last known safe sphere, so a surface is never skipped — at least as robust as plain sphere tracing, while converging in far fewer steps through conservative fields.

Its precondition is that the field never *overstates* distance, which is exactly what #75 pinned down and property-tests. The two changes fit together: over-relaxation is only sound on a conservative field.

## Measured on the compiled shader

Worst-angle filled coverage over an orbit, for a union squeezed in X by `1/ratio` with the box pre-widened so the rendered solid stays ~100mm across (this isolates field *conditioning* from mere thinness):

| conditioning ratio | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| 12.8 (the #76 project) | 11.25% | 11.87% |
| 30 | 1.49% | 12.05% |
| 60 | **0.00%** | 12.42% |
| 120 | **0.00%** | 12.78% |
| 250 | **0.00%** | 11.48% |
| 500 | **0.00%** | 6.06% |

The reported project sits at ratio 12.8, where both marchers largely cope — consistent with the revised "real but modest" severity on the issue. The failure is *total* from ratio 60 upward.

Cost at the worst angle: **0.105 → 0.165 ms/frame** (432x756, ANGLE/Metal) — well inside a frame budget, though a weak integrated GPU will pay more than this. The step cap goes to 1024 purely as headroom; per the analysis on #76 the budget is not what fixes this (384 and 1024 both measure clean), the over-relaxation is.

## Test

#76 noted the algorithm had only been verified by simulating both marchers against the TypeScript evaluator, which cannot see the compiled GLSL — the thing that actually ships. `e2e/marcher-grazing.spec.ts` closes that gap: it drives the real app, orbits to near-edge-on views of the badly-conditioned axis, and asserts the shader still fills the surface.

Validated as a real guard, not a decoration — reverting `SdfMesh.ts` to the old marcher makes it **fail at 0.00% coverage** (elev 20 / azim 90); it passes at 12.78% with the fix. The suite covers both the literal #76 project (kept for regression coverage, though a weak discriminator) and the ratio-120 case that actually separates the two marchers.

The *size* of the improvement is deliberately not asserted — coverage percentages vary with GPU and ANGLE backend, so the floor sits far below every measured passing value and far above a dropout.

## Verification

- `tsc --noEmit` clean
- 258 unit tests pass (18 files)
- 50 e2e tests pass, including the new spec (the one reported failure is the pre-existing documented `text with glyph outlines` divergence)

## Not closing #76

The complete fix is anisotropic marching in the child's local space. This is the incremental mitigation that issue explicitly calls for, so #76 should stay open for the proper fix.
